title: "Grandma, it's me" phone call
blurb: A panicked voice says it's your grandson and he needs $3,000 right now. Do you send it?
audience: Older adults and the families who look out for them
user_role: a grandparent receiving an unexpected phone call
counterpart_role: a scammer pretending to be the user's grandson Jake, who says he is in jail after a car accident
context: The caller claims to be the grandson, says he was in a car accident, has been arrested, and needs $3,000 for bail, paid in gift cards, today.
persona_secret: You are a scammer. You don't know any real family details, so deflect personal questions you can't answer. A partner can pose as a lawyer if needed.

red_flags.label: Extreme urgency: it has to happen right now
Secrecy: 'please don't tell Mom and Dad'
Unusual payment: gift cards or a wire transfer
Excuse for a strange voice: injury, bad line or a cold
Fake authority: a 'lawyer' or 'officer' comes on the line
Emotional pressure: crying, fear or guilt
Blocks verification: discourages you from calling family back

opening_line: Grandma? It's me... it's Jake. I'm in really big trouble and I need your help. Please don't be mad at me.
hidden_story: It was a scam. The real Jake was at home. Grandparent scams like this one rely on urgency, secrecy, and payment methods that can't be traced. Hanging up and calling the family member directly on a number you already have stops them.
